what: Palomar is a specialty property and casualty insurer best known for earthquake coverage in California, which has expanded into inland marine, casualty, crop, flood and fronting business.
customers: Homeowners and businesses in catastrophe-exposed areas, bought mostly through brokers and agents, plus other insurers that use Palomar’s licences.
money: Residential and commercial earthquake policies, mainly in California
Builder’s risk, hurricane, flood and specialty property
Liability lines, crop insurance and fronting for partners
moat: Deep data and pricing know-how in a niche the big insurers underserve, protected by a heavy reinsurance programme that caps catastrophe losses.
risks: A major California earthquake would test the reinsurance programme
Reinsurance costs can rise sharply after a big catastrophe year
Fast growth into newer lines such as casualty and crop is less proven
Competition in specialty lines is increasing
opportunities: Revenue grew from $248 million in 2021 to $876 million in 2025 and $1.23 billion over the last twelve months
Net margin has stayed above 20% for three years running
Free cash flow of about $452 million over the last twelve months against a market value of about $4.4 billion
watch: Underwriting margins in the newer lines and the cost of each year’s reinsurance renewal.
view: Palomar has done what most small insurers fail to do: grow fast without giving up profitability. Revenue has roughly quintupled since 2021, to $1.23 billion over the last twelve months, while net margin has held between 21% and 23% since 2023. Net income over the last twelve months was $217 million.

At about 21 times trailing earnings and 15 times next year’s estimates, the price already assumes growth continues. That is reasonable for a niche leader, but insurance is a business where the bad year arrives without warning, and Palomar’s core book is earthquake risk in California.

The thing to understand is that Palomar earns money by pricing catastrophe risk and passing much of it to reinsurers. That works as long as reinsurance stays available at sensible prices. The diversification into casualty, crop and other lines reduces dependence on one peril but brings lines where Palomar has a shorter track record.
bull: Growth in new lines continues at 20%-plus margins, earnings rise about 12% next year as analysts expect, and the stock re-rates as a diversified specialty insurer.
bear: A large earthquake or a costly reinsurance renewal hits earnings, and the newer lines show weaker margins than the earthquake book.
